correspondence.finding: The actual northeastern beginning follows the minor northern/eastern stream setting into a south-southwest-running valley containing a prominent lobed lake and narrower connected waters. The closer original map shows the stream, lake and downstream valley connections. The modeled line is generalized and locally offset from the detailed channels and shorelines; it must not be read as a surveyed through-lake centreline or an exact official source. No inspected label establishes a separate name for this northern feeder or its lake components.

The northern approach continues south and turns west into the repeatedly labeled Kuujjua River corridor. The official map also prints Kuujjua River on a separate continuation coming from farther east/southeast. That continuation is contextual and unselected. Consequently the mainstem model does not prove that the whole northern beginning itself bears the Kuujjua hydronym.

Below this connection the selection follows the named Kuujjua south, then west around its large eastern bend, and northwest before turning west and southwest again. The characteristic bend sequence, neighboring stream junctions and lake-bearing valley agree with the official map. Burns Lake lies to the southeast on a different lake/stream setting and is not substituted for the selected beginning or treated as a selected through-passage.

The overlapping middle map follows the selection along the named Kuujjua through successive westward bends, then down the prominent southwest-running valley. At the lower middle junction it makes the selected northerly hook within a lake-and-channel setting, turns south and continues west. Large northern lake bodies and southern side approaches remain contextual; their entire water areas are not included merely because they connect to the selected trunk.

The western map continues the same labeled river down the west-southwest corridor, through the long east-west lower lake setting and into a succession of broader connected lake basins that turns northwest and north. The selection is a lake-and-river route here, not one continuously narrow river channel. The DFO figure independently places Tatik Lake, called Fish Lake in its text and caption, in this lower Kuujjua/Minto Inlet setting. Its small historical figure does not settle the detailed naming boundary of each basin in the chain.

After the northward lower lake passage, the selected line bends west along the final outlet valley, directly labeled Kuujjua River, and ends at the southern Minto Inlet shoreline/river-mouth setting. Both the regional NRCan overview and DFO Figure 1 identify Minto Inlet as the receiving-water context. The endpoint is not extended across the inlet or into the separate Prince Albert Sound drainage. Exact present-day shoreline, tidal limit and river-to-inlet naming boundary are not assigned.

The selected beginning is a short eastward feeder south of Cerro Colorado in western Guadalupe y Calvo. It joins the south-southeastward channel labeled Basonopita, with that label repeated farther downstream near the Cerro Chinacas setting. The actual first feeder is not separately named, and the model start is not an official river source. The eastern Baborigame/San José approach is distinct from this selected upstream route.

The Basonopita corridor continues toward the southern municipal margin and the receiving river in northern Badiraguato. There the selected course turns west and then northwest around the Cerro Pelón–Cerro La Ciénega setting along reaches directly labeled Río Sinaloa. The mapped San Javier, El Potrerillos and more southerly Santiago approaches remain side waterways rather than replacement selected headwaters.

The selected northwestward course leaves the northern Badiraguato valley toward the eastern Sinaloa municipal margin, makes the distinctive northern bend, then proceeds southwest and south on the mapped Sinaloa trunk. The Sinaloa relief map supports this approach above Bacurato reservoir; the Juan de Haro river entering from farther north is separate from the selected eastern approach.

The route enters the northward extension of the mapped reservoir labeled Lic. Gustavo Díaz Ordaz (Bacurato), passes through its principal connected river corridor and leaves toward the west. The state map labels the waterbody Presa Gustavo Díaz Ordaz (Bacurato). Reservoir arms and their tributaries are not additional selected paths. Guillermo Blake/El Sabinal to the northwest and Adolfo López Mateos to the southeast belong to different corridors.

Below the reservoir, the line follows the Río Sinaloa valley through the Sinaloa de Leyva setting and southwest toward Bamoa and Guasave. The municipal and state maps distinguish this trunk from the western Ocoroni drainage and from the straight irrigation canals. On the Guasave plain, the selected course follows the directly labeled Río Sinaloa east of Laguna Chamicari and continues through the Guasave settlement setting.

The lower selected reach continues south past the Tamazula–La Brecha–San José de la Brecha corridor, then turns toward the coastal mouth setting at Boca del Río beside Las Glorias. The state and Guasave maps place this terminal at the Gulf of California coast rather than in Laguna Uyaqui, Laguna Jupabampo or the more southerly Playa Colorada lagoon system. The model does not trace every delta distributary or establish a surveyed contemporary shoreline intersection.

The northeastern beginning descends the eastern side of Sierra El Chivato through the stream labeled El Carrizo on the Santa Cruz relief map, then continues southwest. The selected approach is east of the separately mapped Los Alisos and El Represo Enterrado branches; La Mesteña and Tanque Negro are also distinct western approaches. The north-flowing Río Santa Cruz lies on the other side of the upland and is not the selected river. The first modeled vertex is not an official source point, and no separate name is assigned to its short initial headward segment.

On entering the Ímuris coverage, the route matches the southwesterly valley directly labeled Cocospera. It follows the eastern side of Sierra El Pinito and reaches the Comaquito junction setting. El Cazadero, Los Fresnos/Cajón de la Ciéneguita and Las Palomas are separately mapped approaches, not replacement headwaters for the selected modeled line.

At Comaquito the model turns west along the connected northern river junction and continues across the reach explicitly labeled Río Babasac in the Ímuris relief map. P. Comaquito is mapped predominantly south of this junction; the state sheet labels the waterbody Laguna Comaquito. This supports proximity and connection to the Comaquito system, but not a full reservoir traversal or entry into its southern arms. The selected westward river joins the distinct northern Río Bambuto approach near the Ímuris valley and continues southwest toward Magdalena.

The selected line follows the main southwestern valley through Magdalena de Kino into Santa Ana, with the regional state sheet naming the connected river Magdalena and the municipal sheets supporting the actual course. The selected course does not turn southeast into the El Sásabe branch or Presa Ignacio R. Pesqueira (El Yeso). Tacicuri and La Jojoba are other separately mapped approaches. The Río Bambuto upstream branch north of Ímuris is not substituted for the selected Cocospera branch.

Southwest of Santa Ana the model makes its broad southern bend in the eastern Trincheras valley and then runs northwest along the stream directly labeled Magdalena, north of Cerro Trincheras and Cerro Prieto. El Coyotillo, the locally separate El Carrizo tributary and El Sotol enter this middle setting, while the Busani and Tésota approaches remain distinct. These tributary names do not replace the selected main valley route, and the El Carrizo in this middle setting is not the distant headwater El Carrizo.

The northwestward Magdalena continuation reaches the northern Pitiquito corridor and the river locally labeled Asunción, then passes through the Pitiquito–Heroica Caborca setting. State cartography separates its actual southeast approach from the more northerly approach through Altar/Oquitoa and the Sásabe branch. Basin-table occurrences of Concepción were not used to rename the channel, and these generalized maps do not fix a unique Magdalena-to-Asunción transition vertex.

Below Caborca the selected Asunción turns southwest along the northern side of Cordón Lista Blanca, then northwest around the northern side of Sierra El Álamo. The Caborca relief map directly labels this connected river Río Asunción. At its northwestern bend the separately labeled El Coyote approaches from the northeast; the model then takes the Asunción continuation southwest, rather than selecting El Coyote as an alternative upper river. El Bamuri and San Lorenzo to the south are separate coastal approaches.

The final selected reach follows the Asunción southwest across the coastal plain, then southward to the mapped river-mouth setting just southeast of Desemboque on the Gulf of California (Mar de Cortés). The state original shows the narrow coastal connection and Caborca relief pixels support the same outlet corridor. The modeled terminal is at this coastward mouth setting, not at the more southerly Desemboque de los Seris–San Ignacio outlet. No separate estuary name, modern tidal-channel boundary, permanent open mouth or extension across the Gulf is asserted.

The selected western beginning follows the low southern border corridor eastward through a shallow southern bend, then turns northeast toward the Trois-Sauts setting. IBGE maps this connected drainage separately from the Brazilian Uassipein and Mutura approaches to the south/east. The French report calls the upper Oyapock Kérindioutou and its park map also shows a distinct upper name. The selection is not extended to every headwater or to a claimed official source point.

The northeastward upper mainstem matches the Oyapock corridor from Trois-Sauts through the mapped sequence of rapids to Camopi. The French location map distinguishes this river from the more westerly Camopi, and the municipal map supplies the Brazilian-side drainage and settlement context. The model generalizes river islands, bends and rapids rather than representing each local channel.

The two longer western tributary pieces trace the southwestern Camopi approach, its northward and then eastward lower bend, and its junction with the Oyapock at Camopi/Vila Brasil. The park drainage map shows that full connection and the report explicitly identifies Camopi as the left-bank tributary at Camopi bourg. Camopi is a component name, not an alias of the selected border-river mainstem. The initial small branch is not given a separate source name.

The third tributary piece is a short Brazilian-side approach entering the upper river well south of Camopi. Its connection is visible in the municipal drainage, but a distinct hydronym is not securely printed for this short selected reach. Neither the nearby Mutura nor another more distant tributary name is transferred onto it.

Below Camopi/Vila Brasil, the selected mainstem follows the river northeast past the middle border corridor and the Saint-Georges/Oiapoque setting, then the lower northward channel past the Galibi/Jumina vicinity. It ends in the lower estuarine approach before the complete widening into the bay and Atlantic mouth. The separate eastern Uaçá network and the entire downstream bay are not included merely because they belong to the broader drainage description.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
